## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Audio Signal Analysis, Indexing and Transformations
  Official title       Audio signal Analysis, Indexing and Transformations
  Instructors          G. RICHARD, R.BADEAU (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 2 · period 2 (04/01/2027 – 02/04/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 24 h (lectures 14 h, labs 10 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Signal processing
  Language             Lectures are planned in French, with slides in English (master-mva.com)
  Assessment           Papers reading and analysis, with a written report and an oral presentation (master-mva.com); Université Paris-Saclay: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (partial continuous assessment)
  Prerequisites        Basics of signal processing (master-mva.com)
  Organisation         13.5 h of theoretical lectures and 10.5 h of practical sessions (TP) in Matlab, or in Python if preferred (master-mva.com)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics, who knows the Fourier transform and linear filters, and wants to analyse, index, separate and transform real audio signals.

**Empirical first**: two microphones record three people talking at once. No linear demixing matrix can undo a mixture with more sources than sensors, yet the DUET algorithm of [ch. 8](#ch8) raises the signal-to-distortion ratios of the three voices from −4.6, −3.1 and −1.6 dB to 14.7, 10.7 and 14.9 dB.

In the same spirit, two tones closer than the Fourier resolution of a 64-sample frame give a periodogram with two peaks at the wrong frequencies, while ESPRIT ([ch. 10](#ch10)) finds both within 0.0003 cycles per sample.

This course covers four families of audio problems. **Indexing**, or machine listening, extracts descriptors from a recording to recognise its genre, its instruments, its tempo and its bars. **Transformations** change a sound: digital effects, reverberation, time stretching, pitch shifting, and 3D rendering over headphones or loudspeaker arrays.

**Source separation** recovers individual sources from a mixture. **High-resolution spectral analysis** estimates the frequencies of a sum of sinusoids beyond the Fourier limit. The course is taught by Gaël Richard and Roland Badeau (Télécom Paris, per master-mva.com).

It shares tools with [Audio Signal Processing: Time–Frequency Analysis](../s2-audio-time-frequency/index.html), [Algorithms for Speech and Natural Language Processing](../s2-speech-nlp/index.html) and [Machine Learning for Time Series](../s1-time-series/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Compute and invert a short-time Fourier transform, and choose its window, length and hop for a given audio task.
-   Extract MFCC, chroma and spectral descriptors, and build a genre or instrument classifier evaluated without session or artist leakage.
-   Detect onsets, estimate the tempo, track beats by dynamic programming and locate downbeats.
-   Design flangers, phasers, distortions and artificial reverberators, and predict their frequency responses and decay times.
-   Stretch a sound in time and shift its pitch with a phase vocoder, while preserving its spectral envelope.
-   Explain how HRTFs, crosstalk cancellation and wave field synthesis render a sound in space, and compute their limits.
-   Separate determined linear mixtures by independent component analysis, and explain the permutation problem of convolutive mixtures.
-   Separate more sources than microphones with sparse time–frequency models and DUET.
-   Estimate the frequencies, damping factors and amplitudes of sinusoids with Prony, MUSIC and ESPRIT, and select the model order.
-   Read a research paper of the field, reimplement its method and present it critically, as the official assessment asks.

### How to study this module

-   Work through ch. 0 before session 1: it reviews the official prerequisite (basics of signal processing), and every later chapter uses the DFT, windows and the z-transform without warning.
-   After each session, do the exercises listed in its row, then run the code of the chapter and change one parameter (window length, hop, delay, number of sources, signal-to-noise ratio).
-   Listen to what you compute: write the signals of the code to WAV files (`scipy.io.wavfile.write`) and compare them by ear.
-   The code uses NumPy, SciPy and scikit-learn on synthetic signals; every block runs in a few seconds on a laptop.
-   Start a project of the last section after session 4; the official assessment is a paper study with a report and a talk.

## 0. Review: signals, Fourier analysis, filters and random signals {#ch0}

Every chapter of this course computes spectra, filters signals and reasons about noise. This chapter collects the facts it uses, with the two that matter most for audio: the Fourier resolution limit and the leakage of windows.

### The discrete Fourier transform

A digital audio signal is a sequence $x(n)$ sampled at $f_s$ hertz, typically 16 kHz for speech and 44.1 kHz for music. A normalised angular frequency $\omega$ (radians per sample) corresponds to $f = \omega f_s / 2\pi$ hertz.

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — DTFT and DFT]{.tag} The discrete-time Fourier transform of a summable sequence and the discrete Fourier transform of a block of $N$ samples are
$$
X(\omega) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} x(n)\, e^{-i \omega n}, \qquad X(k) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x(n)\, e^{-2 i \pi k n / N}, \quad 0 \le k < N .
$$
The DFT samples the DTFT of the block at the $N$ frequencies $\omega_k = 2\pi k / N$, and the FFT computes it in $O(N \log N)$ operations.
:::

By the sampling theorem, a continuous signal whose spectrum vanishes above $f_s / 2$ is determined by its samples. Frequencies above $f_s / 2$ fold back, or alias, which matters for the distortion effects of ch. 4.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Convolution theorem]{.tag} The DTFT of a convolution is the product of the DTFTs:
$$
y(n) = \sum_{m} h(m)\, x(n - m) \quad \Longrightarrow \quad Y(\omega) = H(\omega)\, X(\omega) .
$$
For the DFT the same identity holds with circular convolution. A linear convolution of lengths $N_x$ and $N_h$ is obtained exactly with DFTs of size at least $N_x + N_h - 1$.

::: proof
Substitute $n = m + p$ in the definition of $Y(\omega)$; the double sum factorises into $\sum_m h(m) e^{-i\omega m} \sum_p x(p) e^{-i\omega p}$. For the DFT, indices are taken modulo $N$. Zero-padding both sequences to $N_x + N_h - 1$ samples removes the wrap-around terms. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Linear filters

::: def
[Definition 0.3 — Linear time-invariant filter]{.tag} A causal filter given by a difference equation,
$$
y(n) = \sum_{p=0}^{P} b_p\, x(n - p) - \sum_{q=1}^{Q} a_q\, y(n - q),
$$
has the transfer function $H(z) = B(z) / A(z)$, with $B(z) = \sum_p b_p z^{-p}$ and $A(z) = 1 + \sum_q a_q z^{-q}$. It is FIR when $Q = 0$ and IIR otherwise.

It is stable when all the poles (roots of $A$) lie strictly inside the unit circle. Its frequency response is $H(e^{i\omega})$, with gain $|H|$ and phase $\arg H$.
:::

### Windows, leakage and resolution

A frame of $N$ samples is the product of the signal with a window $w$ supported on $\{0, \dots, N - 1\}$. By Proposition 0.2, the spectrum of the frame is the spectrum of the signal convolved with that of the window.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — Spectrum of a windowed exponential]{.tag} If $x(n) = \alpha\, e^{i \omega_0 n}$, the windowed frame has the spectrum
$$
X_w(\omega) = \alpha\, W(\omega - \omega_0) .
$$
For the rectangular window, $|W(\omega)| = |\sin(N\omega/2) / \sin(\omega/2)|$: its main lobe has half-width $2\pi/N$ and its first sidelobe is 13 dB below the peak.

For the Hann window $w(n) = \tfrac12 - \tfrac12 \cos(2\pi n / N)$, the main lobe is twice as wide ($4\pi/N$), but the first sidelobe is 31 dB down and the sidelobes decay as $1/\omega^3$, that is 18 dB per octave.

::: proof
For the rectangle, $W(\omega) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} e^{-i\omega n}$ is a geometric sum, equal to $e^{-i\omega(N-1)/2} \sin(N\omega/2) / \sin(\omega/2)$. It vanishes first at $\omega = 2\pi/N$.

The Hann window is a sum of three exponentials, so its transform is a sum of three shifted copies of the rectangular one. The shifts by $\pm 2\pi/N$ cancel the sidelobes to leading order and move the first zero to $4\pi/N$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Two consequences organise the rest of the course.

-   **Resolution.** Two exponentials closer than about one main-lobe half-width merge into one peak. This is the **Rayleigh limit**: a frequency gap of $f_s / N$ hertz for the rectangle. Zero-padding interpolates the DTFT, but it does not resolve anything.
-   **Leakage.** A strong component spreads energy far away through its sidelobes and can hide a weak one. Windows trade main-lobe width (resolution) for sidelobe level (dynamic range).

The code below adds a tone 50 dB below a strong one, 150 Hz away, in a 50 ms frame.

```python
import numpy as np

fs, N = 8000, 400                         # a 50 ms analysis window, fs/N = 20 Hz
n = np.arange(N)
strong = np.cos(2 * np.pi * 1000 * n / fs)
weak = 10 ** (-50 / 20) * np.cos(2 * np.pi * 1150 * n / fs)   # 50 dB below

def level_db(x, w, f0, pad=16):
    X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x * w, pad * N))   # zero padding interpolates only
    f = np.fft.rfftfreq(pad * N, 1 / fs)
    X_db = 20 * np.log10(X / X.max())
    return X_db[np.argmin(np.abs(f - f0))]

for name, w in [("rectangular", np.ones(N)), ("Hann", np.hanning(N))]:
    without = level_db(strong, w, 1150)
    with_ = level_db(strong + weak, w, 1150)
    print(f"{name:12s} level at 1150 Hz: {without:6.1f} dB without the weak tone,"
          f" {with_:6.1f} dB with it")
```

With the rectangular window the level at 1150 Hz is −27.0 dB with or without the weak tone, which stays invisible under a sidelobe. With the Hann window it rises from −62.2 dB to −49.9 dB: the weak tone appears at its true level.

### Random signals

::: def
[Definition 0.5 — Stationary signals and power spectral density]{.tag} A random signal is wide-sense stationary when its mean is constant and its autocorrelation depends only on the lag:
$$
r_x(k) = \mathbb{E}\big[x(n + k)\, \overline{x(n)}\big] .
$$
Its power spectral density is $S_x(\omega) = \sum_k r_x(k)\, e^{-i\omega k}$ (Wiener–Khinchin). White noise of variance $\sigma^2$ has $r_x(k) = \sigma^2 \delta(k)$ and a flat spectrum.
:::

Filtering a stationary signal by $H$ multiplies its spectral density by $|H(e^{i\omega})|^2$. The covariance matrix $\mathbf{R}$ of $L$ consecutive samples is Hermitian, Toeplitz and positive semidefinite.

Chapters 7, 9 and 10 also use two facts from linear algebra. A Hermitian matrix has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues. Any matrix has a singular value decomposition
$$
\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{U} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{V}^H,
$$
and its first $K$ left singular vectors span the column space of its best rank-$K$ approximation.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   The DFT samples the spectrum of a block; convolution becomes a product, circular for the DFT.
-   A filter is stable when its poles lie inside the unit circle; its frequency response is $H(e^{i\omega})$.
-   Windowing convolves the spectrum with the window's transform: main-lobe width limits resolution to about $f_s / N$, sidelobes cause leakage.
-   Stationary signals are described by their autocorrelation or their power spectral density.
:::

## 1. Time–frequency representations and audio features {#ch1}

Audio signals are not stationary: notes start and stop, voices glide. This chapter builds the short-time Fourier transform, proves when it can be inverted, and derives from it the descriptors used for indexing in ch. 2–3.

### The short-time Fourier transform

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Short-time Fourier transform]{.tag} With an analysis window $w$ of length $N$ and a hop of $R$ samples, the STFT of $x$ is
$$
X(m, k) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x(n + mR)\, w(n)\, e^{-2 i \pi k n / N},
$$
for the frame index $m$ and the frequency bin $k$. Its squared modulus $|X(m, k)|^2$ is the **spectrogram**.
:::

The window length sets a trade-off. At 16 kHz, $N = 1024$ gives frames of 64 ms and bins 15.6 Hz apart: good for pitch, poor for drum attacks. Speech analysis typically uses frames of 20–40 ms and music analysis 40–100 ms.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.2 — Overlap-add reconstruction]{.tag} Let $y_m(n)$ be the inverse DFT of frame $m$, multiplied by a synthesis window $w_s$, and placed back at time $mR$ by overlap-add. If the windows satisfy
$$
\sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} w(n - mR)\, w_s(n - mR) = 1 \quad \text{for all } n,
$$
then the overlap-add $\sum_m y_m$ equals $x$ exactly.

::: proof
The inverse DFT of frame $m$ returns $x(n + mR)\, w(n)$ for $0 \le n < N$. After the synthesis window and the shift, frame $m$ contributes at time $n$ the sample
$$
x(n)\, w(n - mR)\, w_s(n - mR) .
$$
Summing over $m$ and using the condition gives $x(n)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For the periodic Hann window and $R = N/4$, the shifted windows sum to 2 and their squares to 3/2. So $w_s = \tfrac{2}{3} w$ reconstructs exactly; the code below normalises by $\sum_m w^2(n - mR)$, which is the same thing.

A *modified* STFT (masked in ch. 8, re-phased in ch. 5) is generally not the STFT of any signal; ch. 11 explains what overlap-add then returns.

### Perceptual scales

The ear resolves low frequencies finely and high frequencies coarsely: its critical bands are about 100 Hz wide below 500 Hz and about a fifth of an octave above. Audio descriptors imitate this with nonlinear frequency scales.

::: def
[Definition 1.3 — Mel scale and mel filterbank]{.tag} The mel scale maps a frequency $f$ in hertz to
$$
\mathrm{mel}(f) = 2595 \log_{10}\Big(1 + \frac{f}{700}\Big) .
$$
A mel filterbank has $J$ triangular filters $H_j(k)$ whose centres are equally spaced in mel; each filter rises from the centre of its left neighbour to its own centre and falls to the centre of its right neighbour. The **log-mel spectrogram** is $\log \sum_k H_j(k)\, |X(m, k)|^2$.
:::

The constant-Q transform follows the same idea with geometrically spaced bins, $f_k = f_{\min}\, 2^{k / b}$ with $b$ bins per octave, so that every bin spans the same musical interval.

::: def
[Definition 1.4 — Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients]{.tag} The MFCCs of frame $m$ are the first coefficients (typically 13) of the type-II discrete cosine transform of the log-mel energies $E_j(m)$:
$$
c_q(m) = \sum_{j=1}^{J} \log E_j(m)\, \cos\Big(\frac{\pi q (j - \tfrac12)}{J}\Big), \qquad q = 0, \dots, 12 .
$$
:::

Why a cosine transform of a logarithm? The answer is the source–filter view of sound production.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.5 — The cepstrum separates source and filter]{.tag} If a frame spectrum factorises as an excitation times a spectral envelope, $X(\omega) = E(\omega)\, H(\omega)$, then
$$
\log |X(\omega)| = \log |E(\omega)| + \log |H(\omega)| .
$$
When $H$ varies slowly with frequency and $E$ is a harmonic comb of spacing $\omega_0$, the inverse Fourier transform of $\log |X|$ (the **cepstrum**) concentrates the envelope at quefrencies below $2\pi / \omega_0$ samples and the excitation at multiples of $2\pi / \omega_0$.

::: proof
The logarithm turns the product into a sum, and the inverse transform is linear. A smooth function of $\omega$ has a transform concentrated near zero. A comb of spacing $\omega_0$ in $\log|E|$ is periodic in $\omega$, so its transform is supported near the multiples of the period $2\pi/\omega_0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Keeping the low quefrencies (liftering) therefore keeps the envelope, which carries timbre and vowel identity, and discards pitch. MFCCs apply the same idea on the mel scale; the cosine transform also decorrelates the log-mel energies of neighbouring filters.

### Descriptors and chroma

::: def
[Definition 1.6 — Spectral and temporal descriptors]{.tag} For a frame with power spectrum $P(k) = |X(m, k)|^2$ and bin frequencies $f_k$:

-   the **spectral centroid** $\sum_k f_k P(k) / \sum_k P(k)$, correlated with perceived brightness;
-   the **roll-off**, the frequency below which 85 % (or 95 %) of the energy lies;
-   the **spectral flux**, the distance between consecutive normalised spectra (ch. 3);
-   the **zero-crossing rate** of the waveform, high for noisy sounds;
-   the **attack time** and the **energy envelope** of a note (ch. 2).
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.7 — Chroma]{.tag} Chroma features fold the spectrum onto the 12 pitch classes of Western music. With a reference $f_{\mathrm{ref}} = 440$ Hz (the class A), bin $k$ goes to the class
$$
p(k) = \mathrm{round}\big(12 \log_2(f_k / f_{\mathrm{ref}})\big) \bmod 12,
$$
and $C_p(m) = \sum_{k : p(k) = p} |X(m, k)|^2$. Chroma is invariant to octave and largely to timbre: it describes harmony.
:::

The code computes an STFT, checks the reconstruction of Proposition 1.2, then extracts MFCCs and chroma from four notes a semitone apart, starting on A3 (220 Hz).

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.fft import dct

fs, N, R = 16000, 1024, 256                  # window 64 ms, hop 16 ms
w = np.hanning(N + 1)[:N]                    # periodic Hann window
print("COLA sum (hop N/4):", np.round(sum(np.roll(w, k * R) for k in range(N // R))[:3], 6))

def stft(x):
    frames = [x[i:i + N] * w for i in range(0, len(x) - N + 1, R)]
    return np.fft.rfft(np.array(frames), axis=1)            # shape (M, N/2 + 1)

def istft(X, length):
    y, norm = np.zeros(length), np.zeros(length)
    for m, frame in enumerate(np.fft.irfft(X, n=N, axis=1)):
        y[m * R:m * R + N] += frame * w                      # synthesis window
        norm[m * R:m * R + N] += w ** 2
    return y / np.maximum(norm, 1e-12)

def mel(f):  return 2595 * np.log10(1 + f / 700)
def imel(m): return 700 * (10 ** (m / 2595) - 1)

def mel_filterbank(n_mels=40, fmin=0.0, fmax=fs / 2):
    edges = imel(np.linspace(mel(fmin), mel(fmax), n_mels + 2))
    f = np.fft.rfftfreq(N, 1 / fs)
    H = np.zeros((n_mels, len(f)))
    for j in range(n_mels):
        lo, c, hi = edges[j], edges[j + 1], edges[j + 2]
        H[j] = np.clip(np.minimum((f - lo) / (c - lo), (hi - f) / (hi - c)), 0, None)
    return H

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
t = np.arange(2 * fs) / fs
f0 = 220 * 2 ** (np.floor(t / 0.5) / 12)                     # four notes, a semitone apart
x = sum(np.sin(2 * np.pi * k * np.cumsum(f0) / fs) / k for k in range(1, 9))
x += 0.01 * rng.standard_normal(len(x))

X = stft(x)
y = istft(X, len(x))
inner = slice(N, len(x) - N)
print("reconstruction error:", f"{np.max(np.abs(x[inner] - y[inner])):.1e}")

logmel = np.log(np.abs(X) ** 2 @ mel_filterbank().T + 1e-10)    # (M, 40)
mfcc = dct(logmel, type=2, norm="ortho", axis=1)[:, :13]
print("frames:", X.shape[0], "| MFCC shape:", mfcc.shape)
f = np.fft.rfftfreq(N, 1 / fs)
pc = np.round(12 * np.log2(np.maximum(f, 1) / 440)) % 12      # pitch class, 0 = A
keep = (f > 50) & (f < 2000)
chroma = np.stack([(np.abs(X[:, keep]) ** 2)[:, pc[keep] == p].sum(1) for p in range(12)], 1)
names = "A A# B C C# D D# E F F# G G#".split()
centres = ((np.arange(4) * 0.5 + 0.25) * fs - N / 2) // R   # one frame inside each note
print("dominant pitch class per note:", [names[np.argmax(chroma[int(m)])] for m in centres])
```

The shifted windows sum to 2, the reconstruction error is $1.1 \times 10^{-15}$ (rounding only), the 2 s signal gives 122 frames of 13 MFCCs, and the chroma follows the notes A, A#, B, C.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   The STFT trades time resolution for frequency resolution through the window length; overlap-add inverts it when the shifted products of analysis and synthesis windows sum to one.
-   Mel and constant-Q scales imitate the frequency resolution of hearing.
-   The cepstrum separates a slowly varying envelope (timbre) from a harmonic excitation (pitch); MFCCs are a mel-scale cepstrum.
-   Spectral descriptors summarise brightness, noisiness and change; chroma summarises harmony.
:::

## 2. Audio indexing I: classifying genres and instruments {#ch2}

Content-based indexing labels a recording from its signal alone: its genre, the instruments playing, the sound events it contains. This chapter builds the classical pipeline on the features of ch. 1 and shows how easily its evaluation can be fooled.

### The bag-of-frames pipeline

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Bag-of-frames classifier]{.tag} A recording is cut into frames of 20–100 ms, each described by a feature vector $\mathbf{x}_m$ (MFCCs, descriptors, chroma).

Features are then integrated over **texture windows** of about 1–5 s, typically by their mean and standard deviation. A classifier labels each window, and window decisions are aggregated (majority vote or summed log-probabilities) into a label for the recording.
:::

The model ignores the order of frames inside a window, hence its name. It works well for timbre-driven tasks (instrument, genre, acoustic scene) and poorly for tasks that depend on temporal structure, such as rhythm, which ch. 3 treats separately.

### Gaussian mixture models

::: def
[Definition 2.2 — GMM classifier]{.tag} Each class $c$ has a density on feature vectors, a mixture of $G$ Gaussians:
$$
p(\mathbf{x} \mid c) = \sum_{g=1}^{G} \pi_{cg}\, \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x};\, \boldsymbol{\mu}_{cg}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{cg}) .
$$
Treating the frames $\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_M$ of a window as independent, the Bayes rule picks
$$
\hat c = \arg\max_c \Big( \log p(c) + \sum_{m=1}^{M} \log p(\mathbf{x}_m \mid c) \Big) .
$$
:::

The independence assumption is false (consecutive frames overlap), which makes the posterior probabilities overconfident, but the argmax is often still good.

The class densities are fitted to the training frames of each class by the EM algorithm, whose updates and monotonicity are proved in ch. 11.

### Discriminative classifiers and feature selection

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — Support vector machine]{.tag} A kernel SVM labels a feature vector by the sign of
$$
g(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i\, K(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}) + b,
$$
where the $\alpha_i \ge 0$ solve a convex quadratic problem that maximises the margin, and $K$ is often the Gaussian kernel. Several classes are handled by one-versus-one or one-versus-all votes. The theory is in [Kernel Methods](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html).
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.4 — Fisher discriminant ratio]{.tag} With hundreds of candidate descriptors, a simple filter keeps those with a large ratio of between-class to within-class spread. For one feature, two classes with means $\mu_1, \mu_2$ and variances $\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2$,
$$
F = \frac{(\mu_1 - \mu_2)^2}{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2} .
$$
:::

### Genre recognition and instrument identification

::: ex
[Example 2.5 — Genre recognition]{.tag} Tzanetakis and Cook (2002) introduced automatic genre classification with three feature sets: timbral texture (centroid, roll-off, flux, zero crossings, MFCCs), rhythmic content (a beat histogram built from the autocorrelation of ch. 3) and pitch content. Their data set, GTZAN, has 1000 excerpts of 30 s in 10 genres.

Sturm (2014) later showed that GTZAN contains repeated excerpts, mislabelled ones and many excerpts by the same artists. Part of the published accuracies measured artist recognition or plain duplication rather than genre.
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.6 — Timbre descriptors for instruments]{.tag} Instrument recognition relies on descriptors of timbre, for example:

-   the **attack time** of the energy envelope (short for plucked strings and percussion);
-   the **spectral centroid** and its evolution;
-   the **odd-to-even harmonic energy ratio**, high for the clarinet, whose cylindrical bore weakens even harmonics;
-   the **inharmonicity** of partials (pianos, bells) and MFCC statistics.

In polyphonic music, Essid, Richard and David (2006) classify combinations of instruments, organised in a hierarchical taxonomy learned from the data.
:::

### Evaluating an indexing system

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.7 — Artist, album and session filters]{.tag} Suppose that each recording session (artist, album, room, microphone) adds to all its excerpts a signature that a classifier can learn. Suppose also that sessions are nested in classes, as albums are in genres.

Then a random split of excerpts into training and test sets lets the classifier use the signature, and its test accuracy overestimates its accuracy on new sessions. Splitting by session (an **artist filter**) removes this bias.

::: proof
Under a random split, a test excerpt from session $s$ has, with high probability, training excerpts from the same session and thus the same label. A rule that recognises sessions, then outputs their label, is then correct on the test set without using any class information. On new sessions its signature carries no label information, so the same rule falls to chance level on that part. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The code builds three synthetic instruments recorded in 18 sessions (one instrument per session, each with its own random equaliser), describes each note by the mean and standard deviation of 13 MFCCs, and compares a random split with a session-disjoint split.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.fft import dct
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, StratifiedGroupKFold

fs, N, R = 16000, 512, 256
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
w = np.hanning(N + 1)[:N]
f = np.fft.rfftfreq(N, 1 / fs)
mel = lambda x: 2595 * np.log10(1 + x / 700)
edges = 700 * (10 ** (np.linspace(0, mel(fs / 2), 42) / 2595) - 1)
H = np.array([np.clip(np.minimum((f - a) / (b - a), (c - f) / (c - b)), 0, None)
              for a, b, c in zip(edges[:-2], edges[1:-1], edges[2:])])   # 40 mel filters

def note(kind, f0, eq):
    """Synthetic note: harmonic amplitudes and envelope depend on the instrument."""
    t = np.arange(int(0.5 * fs)) / fs
    k = np.arange(1, 21)
    amp = [np.where(k % 2 == 1, 1 / k, 0.3 / k),       # 'clarinet': weak even harmonics
           1 / k,                                       # 'bowed string': all harmonics
           1 / k ** 1.5][kind]                          # 'flute': steeper spectral slope
    amp = amp * eq(k * f0) * (k * f0 < fs / 2)          # recording-session colouring
    attack = (0.06, 0.12, 0.04)[kind] * np.exp(0.3 * rng.standard_normal())
    env = np.minimum(t / attack, 1) * np.exp(-t * (1.0, 0.5, 2.0)[kind])
    x = env * (amp[:, None] * np.sin(2 * np.pi * np.outer(k, f0 * t)
                                     + rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, (20, 1)))).sum(0)
    return x + (0.002, 0.01, 0.03)[kind] * env * rng.standard_normal(len(t))

def features(x):
    frames = np.array([x[i:i + N] * w for i in range(0, len(x) - N, R)])
    P = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(frames, axis=1)) ** 2
    mfcc = dct(np.log(P @ H.T + 1e-10), norm="ortho", axis=1)[:, 1:14]
    return np.concatenate([mfcc.mean(0), mfcc.std(0)])  # temporal integration: 26 numbers

X, y, groups = [], [], []
for s in range(18):                                     # 18 sessions, one instrument each
    kind = s % 3
    a, ph = rng.standard_normal(4), rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, 4)
    eq = lambda fr, a=a, ph=ph: np.exp(0.4 * sum(a[j] * np.cos((j + 1) * np.log2(fr / 100) + ph[j])
                                                 for j in range(4)))
    for _ in range(20):
        f0 = 196 * 2 ** (rng.integers(0, 19) / 12)      # G3 to C#5
        X.append(features(note(kind, f0, eq))); y.append(kind); groups.append(s)
X, y, groups = np.array(X), np.array(y), np.array(groups)

def gmm_predict(Xtr, ytr, Xte, k=2):                    # one GMM per class + Bayes rule
    sc = StandardScaler().fit(Xtr)
    L = [GaussianMixture(k, covariance_type="diag", random_state=0)
         .fit(sc.transform(Xtr[ytr == c])).score_samples(sc.transform(Xte)) for c in range(3)]
    return np.argmax(L, axis=0)                         # equal priors

def svm_predict(Xtr, ytr, Xte):
    return make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(C=10)).fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte)

splits = {"random split": StratifiedKFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=0).split(X, y),
          "session-disjoint": StratifiedGroupKFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=0).split(X, y, groups)}
for split, folds in splits.items():
    folds = list(folds)
    for name, predict in [("GMM", gmm_predict), ("SVM", svm_predict)]:
        acc = [np.mean(predict(X[tr], y[tr], X[te]) == y[te]) for tr, te in folds]
        print(f"{split:16s} {name}: accuracy {np.mean(acc):.3f}")
```

The random split reports 0.828 for the GMM and 0.983 for the SVM. On sessions never seen in training, the accuracies drop to 0.758 and 0.925: the gap is the part of the score that recognised sessions rather than instruments.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   Bag-of-frames indexing extracts frame features, integrates them over texture windows and classifies them; GMMs with the Bayes rule and SVMs are the classical classifiers.
-   Genre recognition mixes timbre, rhythm and pitch features; instrument recognition relies on timbre descriptors such as attack time and the odd-to-even harmonic ratio.
-   Any shared signature (artist, album, session) must be confined to one side of the split, or the accuracy is inflated.
:::

## 3. Audio indexing II: onsets, tempo, beats and downbeats {#ch3}

Rhythm is the temporal side of indexing: where notes start, how fast the pulse is, where each beat falls and where each bar begins. The chain goes from an onset detection function to a tempo, then to beat times and downbeats.

### Onset detection

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Spectral-flux onset detection function]{.tag} With the STFT magnitudes $|X(m, k)|$ and a compression constant $\gamma > 0$, the log-spectral flux is
$$
O(m) = \sum_k \Big[ \log\big(1 + \gamma |X(m, k)|\big) - \log\big(1 + \gamma |X(m - 1, k)|\big) \Big]_+ ,
$$
where $[u]_+ = \max(u, 0)$ keeps energy increases only. Onsets are the peaks of $O$ above an adaptive threshold, such as a local median plus a constant.
:::

The logarithm makes soft and loud notes comparable, and the half-wave rectification ignores decays. Bello et al. (2005) compare this function with energy-, phase- and complex-domain variants.

### Tempo estimation

::: def
[Definition 3.2 — Tempo by autocorrelation]{.tag} Let the onset function be sampled at $F$ frames per second, with mean removed. Its autocorrelation $r(\ell) = \sum_m O(m)\, O(m + \ell)$ peaks at lags that are multiples of the beat period. The tempo estimate in beats per minute (BPM) is
$$
\hat T = \frac{60\, F}{\ell^\star}, \qquad \ell^\star = \arg\max_{\ell} \; r(\ell)\, \pi(\ell),
$$
where the prior $\pi$ favours lags near 120 BPM, for example a Gaussian in $\log_2$ of the tempo.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.3 — Octave errors]{.tag} If $O$ is periodic with period $P$ frames, then $r$ is periodic with period $P$ and takes the same value at every multiple of $P$. An unweighted maximisation over lags cannot distinguish the tempo from its half, a third, and so on.

If moreover the first beat of each bar is accented, with bars of $3P$ or $4P$ frames, then $r$ has larger peaks at multiples of the bar period.

::: proof
Shifting the lag by $P$ shifts one factor of each product by a period, which leaves it unchanged; so $r(\ell + P) = r(\ell)$ and $r(kP) = r(0)$. Accents repeating every bar add a component of period $3P$ or $4P$ to $O$, whose autocorrelation peaks at multiples of the bar. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This is why the prior $\pi$ is needed, and why tempo errors by a factor 2 or 3 are counted separately in evaluations. Comb-filter banks (Scheirer, 1998) and Fourier tempograms (Grosche and Müller, 2011) are alternatives to the autocorrelation; all face the same ambiguity.

### Beat tracking by dynamic programming

::: def
[Definition 3.4 — Beat-tracking objective (Ellis, 2007)]{.tag} Given the onset function $O$ (normalised to unit variance) and the beat period $\tau$ in frames, a beat sequence $t_1 < \dots < t_B$ scores
$$
C(t_1, \dots, t_B) = \sum_{i=1}^{B} O(t_i) + \alpha \sum_{i=2}^{B} F(t_i - t_{i-1}), \qquad F(\Delta) = -\Big(\log \frac{\Delta}{\tau}\Big)^2 .
$$
The first sum rewards beats on onsets; the second penalises intervals far from $\tau$, with a tightness $\alpha$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.5 — Exact optimisation]{.tag} Let $C^\star(t)$ be the best score of a beat sequence ending at frame $t$. Then
$$
C^\star(t) = O(t) + \max\Big(0,\; \max_{\tau/2 \le \Delta \le 2\tau} \big[ \alpha F(\Delta) + C^\star(t - \Delta) \big]\Big),
$$
and back-tracking from the best final frame recovers an optimal sequence. With $T$ frames the cost is $O(T \tau)$.

::: proof
A sequence ending at $t$ is either the single beat $t$ or a sequence ending at some $t - \Delta$ followed by $t$. The score is additive along the sequence, so the best extension uses the best sequence ending at $t - \Delta$ (optimal substructure).

Storing the maximising $\Delta$ for each $t$ allows back-tracking. Each frame examines $O(\tau)$ predecessors. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The restriction to $\Delta \in [\tau/2, 2\tau]$ is part of the model: a slowly changing tempo is followed, but a tempo change by more than a factor 2 is not.

### Downbeat estimation

::: def
[Definition 3.6 — Meter, bar position and downbeats]{.tag} In a meter of $B$ beats per bar (often $B = 4$), each beat has a **bar position** $\phi \in \{0, \dots, B - 1\}$; the beats with $\phi = 0$ are the **downbeats**.

Given beats $t_1, t_2, \dots$, a simple estimator picks the phase
$$
\hat p = \arg\max_{p \in \{0, \dots, B-1\}} \frac{1}{|I_p|} \sum_{i \in I_p} D(t_i), \qquad I_p = \{ i : i \equiv p \bmod B \},
$$
for a downbeat salience $D$: low-frequency onsets (bass drum, bass notes) or harmonic change measured on chroma.
:::

Probabilistic models make the bar position a hidden state that advances with each beat, decoded by the Viterbi algorithm (Klapuri, Eronen and Astola, 2006). Current systems learn the salience with neural networks and decode beats and downbeats jointly (Böck, Krebs and Widmer, 2016; Durand et al., 2017).

### Evaluation

A detected beat is correct if it lies within ±70 ms of an annotated one, and precision, recall and their harmonic mean, the F-measure, follow. Tempo accuracy is reported with a 4 % tolerance, with or without accepting factors 2 and 3. The `mir_eval` library (Raffel et al., 2014) implements these measures.

The code synthesises 10 bars of a drum pattern at 128 BPM with 5 ms timing jitter (kick drum on beat 1 and between beats 2 and 3, snare on beats 2 and 4, hi-hat on eighth notes), then runs the whole chain.

```python
import numpy as np

fs, N, R = 16000, 1024, 160                       # ODF frame rate fs/R = 100 Hz
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
bpm, n_bars = 128, 10
beat = 60 / bpm
t = np.arange(int((4 * n_bars + 1) * beat * fs)) / fs
x = 0.003 * rng.standard_normal(len(t))

def hit(t0, kind):
    i = int(t0 * fs); L = int(0.25 * fs); tt = np.arange(L) / fs
    if kind == "kick":  s = np.sin(2 * np.pi * (50 + 80 * np.exp(-tt / 0.03)) * tt) * np.exp(-tt / 0.12)
    if kind == "snare": s = 0.5 * rng.standard_normal(L) * np.exp(-tt / 0.06)
    if kind == "hat":   s = 0.15 * np.diff(rng.standard_normal(L + 1)) * np.exp(-tt / 0.02)
    x[i:i + L] += s[:len(x) - i]

beats = []
for b in range(4 * n_bars):
    tb = b * beat + 0.005 * rng.standard_normal()   # 5 ms human timing jitter
    beats.append(tb)
    if b % 4 == 0: hit(tb, "kick")                  # kick on beat 1 ...
    if b % 4 == 1: hit(tb + beat / 2, "kick")       # ... and on the "and" of 2
    if b % 2 == 1: hit(tb, "snare")                 # snare on 2 and 4
    hit(tb, "hat"); hit(tb + beat / 2, "hat")       # eighth-note hi-hats
beats = np.array(beats)

# 1. Onset detection function: half-wave rectified log-spectral flux
w = np.hanning(N)
S = np.abs(np.array([np.fft.rfft(x[i:i + N] * w) for i in range(0, len(x) - N, R)]))
L = np.log1p(100 * S)
odf = np.maximum(np.diff(L, axis=0), 0).sum(1)
odf = np.concatenate([[0], (odf - odf.mean()) / odf.std()])
times = (np.arange(len(odf)) * R + N / 2) / fs

# 2. Tempo: autocorrelation weighted by a log-Gaussian prior around 120 BPM
lags = np.arange(25, 101)                           # 60 to 240 BPM at 100 frames/s
ac = np.array([odf[:-l] @ odf[l:] for l in lags])
prior = np.exp(-0.5 * np.log2(6000 / lags / 120) ** 2)
lag = lags[np.argmax(ac * prior)]
print(f"tempo estimate: {6000 / lag:.1f} BPM (true {bpm})")

# 3. Beat tracking by dynamic programming (Ellis, 2007)
alpha, tau = 100.0, lag
C, back = odf.copy(), np.zeros(len(odf), int)
for n in range(len(odf)):
    prev = np.arange(n - 2 * tau, n - tau // 2 + 1)
    prev = prev[prev >= 0]
    if len(prev):
        score = C[prev] - alpha * np.log((n - prev) / tau) ** 2
        k = np.argmax(score); C[n] += score[k]; back[n] = prev[k]
n = np.argmax(C[-2 * tau:]) + len(C) - 2 * tau
path = [n]
while back[path[-1]] > 0: path.append(back[path[-1]])
est = times[np.array(path[::-1])]

def f_measure(est, ref, tol=0.07):
    hits = sum(np.min(np.abs(ref - e)) < tol for e in est)
    p, r = hits / len(est), hits / len(ref)
    return 2 * p * r / (p + r)
print(f"beats found: {len(est)} (true {len(beats)}), F-measure at 70 ms: {f_measure(est, beats):.3f}")

# 4. Downbeat: the bar position whose beats carry the most low-frequency onset energy
low = np.maximum(np.diff(L[:, :8], axis=0), 0).sum(1)       # 0 to 125 Hz
energy = np.interp(est, times[1:], low)
phase = np.argmax([energy[p::4].mean() for p in range(4)])
down_est, down_ref = est[phase::4], beats[::4]
print(f"downbeats: {len(down_est)} estimated, F-measure at 70 ms: {f_measure(down_est, down_ref):.3f}")
```

The autocorrelation peaks at a lag of 47 frames, that is 127.7 BPM. The dynamic programme finds 39 of the 40 beats (F-measure 0.987), and the low-frequency salience selects the right bar position (downbeat F-measure 0.947). The simplified code always keeps the best predecessor, a slight departure from the $\max(0, \cdot)$ of Proposition 3.5.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   The log-spectral flux, half-wave rectified, is a robust onset detection function.
-   Its autocorrelation reveals the beat period, up to octave errors that a tempo prior resolves.
-   Ellis's objective trades onset strength against regular intervals, and dynamic programming optimises it exactly.
-   Downbeats are the beats of a fixed bar position, chosen by a salience such as bass onsets or harmonic change; evaluation uses F-measures with a 70 ms tolerance.
:::

## 4. Digital audio effects {#ch4}

Most studio effects are small linear or nonlinear systems whose behaviour can be predicted from their transfer function. This chapter builds the delay-based effects, the phaser, distortion and artificial reverberation from the filters of ch. 0.

### Comb filters, flanger and chorus

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Comb filters]{.tag} With a delay of $D$ samples and a gain $g$, the feedforward and feedback comb filters are
$$
y(n) = x(n) + g\, x(n - D), \qquad y(n) = x(n) + g\, y(n - D),
$$
with transfer functions $1 + g z^{-D}$ and $1 / (1 - g z^{-D})$. The feedback comb is stable if and only if $|g| < 1$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Notches and peaks]{.tag} The feedforward comb has the squared gain
$$
|H(e^{i\omega})|^2 = 1 + g^2 + 2 g \cos(\omega D) .
$$
For $0 < g \le 1$ it has notches of gain $1 - g$ and maxima of gain $1 + g$ at the frequencies
$$
f_{\text{notch}} = \frac{(2k + 1) f_s}{2D}, \qquad f_{\text{max}} = \frac{k f_s}{D}, \qquad k = 0, 1, \dots
$$
The feedback comb has peaks of gain $1 / (1 - g)$ at the frequencies $k f_s / D$.

::: proof
Expand $|1 + g e^{-i\omega D}|^2$. The cosine equals $-1$ when $\omega D = (2k + 1)\pi$ and $+1$ when $\omega D = 2k\pi$.

For the feedback comb, $|1 - g e^{-i\omega D}|$ is smallest, equal to $1 - g$, when $\omega D = 2k\pi$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 4.3 — Flanger, chorus and vibrato]{.tag} A **flanger** is a feedforward comb whose delay is swept by a low-frequency oscillator (LFO), typically between 0 and 10 ms at 0.1–1 Hz:
$$
y(n) = x(n) + g\, x\big(n - D(n)\big) .
$$
The fractional delay is interpolated, for example linearly between the two nearest samples. A **chorus** uses longer delays (10–30 ms) with a slow random modulation and several voices; a **vibrato** outputs the modulated delayed signal alone.
:::

By Proposition 4.2 the flanger's notches are harmonically spaced and sweep together. A delay varying at the rate $D'(t)$ also scales the instantaneous frequency by $1 - D'(t)$: this Doppler effect is the pitch modulation of vibrato and chorus.

### Phaser

::: def
[Definition 4.4 — All-pass section and phaser]{.tag} For a real $a$ with $|a| < 1$, the first-order all-pass section is
$$
A(z) = \frac{a + z^{-1}}{1 + a z^{-1}} .
$$
A **phaser** mixes the input with its output through $M$ cascaded sections, $y = \tfrac12 (x + A^M x)$, and modulates $a$ with an LFO.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.5 — Phaser notches]{.tag} The all-pass section has unit gain at every frequency, and its phase decreases continuously from $0$ at $\omega = 0$ to $-\pi$ at $\omega = \pi$.

Consequently the phaser has a notch wherever the phase of $A^M$ is an odd multiple of $-\pi$. For even $M$ there are $M/2$ notches, not harmonically spaced, which move with $a$.

::: proof
Since $a$ is real, $a + e^{-i\omega} = e^{-i\omega}(1 + a e^{i\omega})$, the product of a unit-modulus factor and the conjugate of the denominator; so $|A(e^{i\omega})| = 1$.

At $\omega = 0$, $A = 1$; at $\omega = \pi$, $A = -1$. The phase is continuous in $\omega$, and its derivative is negative for $|a| < 1$ (the group delay of a stable all-pass is positive).

The total phase of $A^M$ thus covers $[-M\pi, 0]$, and $1 + e^{i M \varphi} = 0$ exactly when $M\varphi$ is an odd multiple of $-\pi$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Distortion

::: def
[Definition 4.6 — Memoryless distortion]{.tag} A waveshaper applies a fixed nonlinear function to each sample, $y(n) = f(x(n))$: soft clipping $f(x) = \tanh(\kappa x)$, hard clipping to $[-1, 1]$, or a polynomial. Valve and transistor stages are often modelled by an asymmetric $f$, possibly between linear filters.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.7 — Harmonics and aliasing]{.tag} Let $x(n) = A \cos(\omega_0 n)$.

1.  The output $f(A \cos\theta)$, a $2\pi$-periodic function of $\theta = \omega_0 n$, contains only harmonics $k\omega_0$; if $f$ is odd, only odd harmonics.
2.  If $f$ is a polynomial of degree $d$, the harmonics stop at $d\,\omega_0$; the Chebyshev polynomial $T_k$ maps $\cos\theta$ to $\cos(k\theta)$.
3.  A harmonic above the Nyquist frequency aliases to $|k\omega_0 - 2\pi m|$, for the integer $m$ that brings it into $[0, \pi]$; it is in general inharmonic.

::: proof
(1) An even, $2\pi$-periodic function of $\theta$ has a cosine series in $k\theta$. If $f$ is odd, replacing $\theta$ by $\theta + \pi$ changes the sign of the output, which cancels every even coefficient.

(2) Powers $\cos^j\theta$ with $j \le d$ expand into $\cos(k\theta)$, $k \le j$; and $T_k(\cos\theta) = \cos k\theta$ is the definition of $T_k$.

(3) The samples of $\cos(k\omega_0 n)$ do not change when $2\pi m$ is subtracted from the frequency. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Since $\tanh$ is not a polynomial, its harmonics never stop, and digital distortion is computed at an oversampled rate, then low-pass filtered and decimated.

### Artificial reverberation

::: def
[Definition 4.8 — Room impulse response and reverberation time]{.tag} A room impulse response contains the direct path, sparse early reflections (the first 50–80 ms) and a dense late reverberation whose energy decays exponentially. The reverberation time $T_{60}$ is the time for that energy to decay by 60 dB.

Sabine's formula estimates it from the volume $V$ (m³) and the absorption area $A = \sum_i S_i \alpha_i$ (m²), the sum of the wall areas $S_i$ weighted by their absorption coefficients $\alpha_i$:
$$
T_{60} \approx 0.161\, \frac{V}{A} \ \text{seconds} .
$$
:::

For a 10 × 8 × 4 m room with $\alpha = 0.2$ everywhere, $V = 320$ m³ and $A = 0.2 \times 304 = 60.8$ m², so
$$
T_{60} \approx 0.85 \text{ s}.
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.9 — Comb gain for a reverberation time]{.tag} A feedback comb of delay $D$ decays by 60 dB in $T_{60}$ seconds if and only if
$$
g = 10^{-3 D / (T_{60} f_s)} .
$$

::: proof
Its impulse response equals $g^j$ at $n = jD$, so the level drops by $-20 \log_{10} g$ dB every $D / f_s$ seconds. Requiring a drop of 60 dB in $T_{60}$ seconds gives $-20 \log_{10} g = 60 D / (T_{60} f_s)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.10 — Schroeder all-pass]{.tag} The filter $H(z) = (-g + z^{-D}) / (1 - g z^{-D})$, with $|g| < 1$, has unit gain at every frequency, while its impulse response is a train of echoes every $D$ samples.

::: proof
On the unit circle, set $u = e^{-i\omega D}$; then $|{-g} + u| = |u|\,|1 - g \bar u| = |1 - g u|$ since $g$ is real, so the numerator and the denominator have equal modulus. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Schroeder's reverberator (1962) combines both: four feedback combs in parallel, with mutually prime delays of 30–45 ms tuned by Proposition 4.9, followed by two all-pass filters of a few milliseconds that multiply the echo density without colouring the spectrum.

Modern reverberators replace the parallel combs by a feedback delay network, in which an orthogonal matrix mixes the outputs of several delay lines, and studios also convolve with measured impulse responses; both are treated in ch. 11.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import lfilter, freqz

fs = 16000
# 1. Flanger at one instant: y = x + g x(n - D), D = 2 ms -> notches at odd multiples of 250 Hz
D, g = int(0.002 * fs), 0.9
f, Hc = freqz(np.r_[1, np.zeros(D - 1), g], worN=8192, fs=fs)
notch = f[1:-1][(np.abs(Hc[1:-1]) < np.abs(Hc[:-2])) & (np.abs(Hc[1:-1]) < np.abs(Hc[2:]))]
print("flanger notches (Hz):", np.round(notch[:4]))

# 2. Phaser: y = (x + A(z) x) / 2 with 4 first-order all-pass sections
a = -0.6
num, den = np.array([1.0]), np.array([1.0])
for _ in range(4):
    num, den = np.convolve(num, [a, 1]), np.convolve(den, [1, a])
f, A = freqz(num, den, worN=8192, fs=fs)
P = np.abs(1 + A) / 2
notch = f[1:-1][(P[1:-1] < P[:-2]) & (P[1:-1] < P[2:])]
print("all-pass |A| in [", np.abs(A).min().round(6), ",", np.abs(A).max().round(6), "]")
print("phaser notches (Hz):", np.round(notch))

# 3. Distortion: tanh soft clipping of a 500 Hz tone, harmonic levels
n = np.arange(fs)
y = np.tanh(4 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 500 * n / fs))
Y = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(y * np.hanning(fs)))
lev = [20 * np.log10(Y[500 * k] / Y[500]) for k in range(2, 8)]
print("harmonics 2..7 (dB re fundamental):", np.round(lev, 1))

# 4. Schroeder reverberator: 4 parallel combs + 2 all-pass, target T60 = 1.5 s
T60 = 1.5
x = np.zeros(2 * fs); x[0] = 1.0
wet = np.zeros_like(x)
for ms in (29.7, 37.1, 41.1, 43.7):
    d = int(ms * fs / 1000)
    gc = 10 ** (-3 * d / (T60 * fs))          # -60 dB after T60 seconds
    wet += lfilter([1.0], np.r_[1, np.zeros(d - 1), -gc], x)
for ms, ga in ((5.0, 0.7), (1.7, 0.7)):
    d = int(ms * fs / 1000)
    wet = lfilter(np.r_[-ga, np.zeros(d - 1), 1], np.r_[1, np.zeros(d - 1), -ga], wet)
edc = 10 * np.log10(np.cumsum(wet[::-1] ** 2)[::-1] / np.sum(wet ** 2))  # Schroeder integration
i5, i35 = np.argmax(edc < -5), np.argmax(edc < -35)
print(f"measured T60 (from the -5 to -35 dB decay): {2 * (i35 - i5) / fs:.2f} s")
```

The flanger's notches fall at 250, 750, 1250 and 1750 Hz, as Proposition 4.2 predicts for a 2 ms delay. The four all-pass sections have unit gain and give 2 notches (525 and 2766 Hz).

The tanh distortion has only odd harmonics, at −11.3, −18.8 and −25.7 dB for the 3rd, 5th and 7th; the even ones sit at the numerical floor (below −190 dB). The reverberator decays with the target time of 1.50 s, measured on Schroeder's backward-integrated energy curve (ch. 11).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   Comb filters have harmonically spaced notches or peaks; sweeping their delay gives flanging, longer modulated delays give chorus.
-   All-pass sections change only the phase; mixed with the dry signal, $M$ of them give $M/2$ movable, inharmonic notches: the phaser.
-   A memoryless nonlinearity creates harmonics, odd ones only if it is odd; harmonics above Nyquist alias unless the effect runs oversampled.
-   Schroeder's reverberator combines feedback combs tuned by $g = 10^{-3D/(T_{60} f_s)}$ with all-pass diffusers of unit gain.
:::

## 5. Time-scale, pitch and timbre modifications {#ch5}

Playing a recording faster raises its pitch: duration and frequency are coupled. This chapter decouples them, first in time (time-scale modification), then in pitch, then in timbre, by working on the STFT of ch. 1 and on the spectral envelope.

### Resampling couples time and pitch

::: prop
[Proposition 5.1 — Resampling]{.tag} Playing a signal at the rate $\beta f_s$ instead of $f_s$ (equivalently, resampling it by $1/\beta$) gives
$$
y(t) = x(\beta t) .
$$
Every frequency is multiplied by $\beta$ and the duration is divided by $\beta$: substitute $\beta t$ for $t$ in $\cos(2\pi f t)$.
:::

A pitch shift by $s$ semitones uses $\beta = 2^{s/12}$; four semitones (a major third) give $\beta = 1.26$. To keep the duration, the signal must first be stretched by $\beta$ without changing its pitch.

### Time-scale modification by overlap-add

::: def
[Definition 5.2 — Overlap-add time-scale modification]{.tag} Frames are taken every $R_a$ samples and overlap-added every $R_s = \alpha R_a$ samples, which multiplies the duration by $\alpha$.

Plain overlap-add breaks the periodicity of the waveform at each frame junction. **WSOLA** shifts each analysis frame by up to $\pm\Delta$ samples to maximise its cross-correlation with the natural continuation of the previous frame. **PSOLA** places the frames pitch-synchronously, which suits monophonic speech.
:::

These time-domain methods work well on speech and single voices, and less well on polyphonic music, where no single shift can align every component. The phase vocoder works per frequency bin instead.

### The phase vocoder

::: def
[Definition 5.3 — Phase vocoder]{.tag} Let $\varphi(m, k)$ be the phase of the STFT with hop $R_a$ at the bin frequency $\omega_k = 2\pi k / N$. Let $\operatorname{princarg}$ reduce an angle to $(-\pi, \pi]$.

The instantaneous frequency of bin $k$ is estimated as
$$
\hat\omega(m, k) = \omega_k + \frac{1}{R_a}\, \operatorname{princarg}\big(\varphi(m, k) - \varphi(m - 1, k) - \omega_k R_a\big) .
$$
The synthesis phases advance at the synthesis hop:
$$
\psi(m, k) = \psi(m - 1, k) + R_s\, \hat\omega(m, k) .
$$
The modified STFT, with magnitude $|X(m, k)|$ and phase $\psi(m, k)$, is inverted by overlap-add every $R_s$ samples.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.4 — Exactness for a stationary sinusoid]{.tag} Let $x(n) = A\cos(\omega_0 n + \phi_0)$ and let bin $k$ lie in the main lobe of $\omega_0$, with no other component nearby. If
$$
|\omega_0 - \omega_k|\, R_a < \pi,
$$
then $\hat\omega(m, k) = \omega_0$ exactly, up to the negligible leakage of the negative-frequency image. For the Hann window, whose main lobe has half-width $4\pi/N$, the condition holds over the whole lobe when $R_a \le N/4$.

::: proof
By Proposition 0.4, near $\omega_0$ the STFT of frame $m$ is
$$
X(m, k) = \tfrac{A}{2}\, e^{i(\omega_0 m R_a + \phi_0)}\, W(\omega_k - \omega_0) .
$$
The window term does not depend on $m$, so the phase advances by exactly $\omega_0 R_a$ between frames, modulo $2\pi$.

Subtracting $\omega_k R_a$ leaves $(\omega_0 - \omega_k) R_a$ modulo $2\pi$. When this lies in $(-\pi, \pi)$, the function $\operatorname{princarg}$ returns it unchanged. Dividing by $R_a$ gives the offset to the bin frequency.

On the main lobe, $|\omega_0 - \omega_k| < 4\pi / N$, so $R_a \le N/4$ gives a product below $\pi$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Each bin is thus re-synthesised at its true frequency with a phase consistent at the new hop. The method still smears transients and adds a reverberant "phasiness", because the phases of neighbouring bins of one partial drift apart. **Phase locking** (Laroche and Dolson, 1999) propagates the phase of each spectral peak and keeps the bins around it locked to it.

### Pitch shifting and the spectral envelope

::: def
[Definition 5.5 — Pitch shifting]{.tag} To shift the pitch by the factor $\beta$ at constant duration, stretch the signal in time by $\alpha = \beta$ with the phase vocoder, then resample it by $1/\beta$ (Proposition 5.1). The two duration changes cancel, and every frequency is multiplied by $\beta$.
:::

This moves the spectral envelope along with the partials: the formants of a voice shift too, and a voice raised by an octave sounds like a cartoon character. Preserving timbre requires the source–filter view of Proposition 1.5.

::: def
[Definition 5.6 — Source–filter model and envelope-preserving modifications]{.tag} Model each frame as $X(\omega) = H(\omega)\, E(\omega)$: a smooth spectral envelope $H$ (the formants, the timbre) times an excitation $E$ (the partials, the pitch).

-   **Envelope-preserving pitch shift**: estimate $H$, divide it out, shift the pitch of $E$, multiply by the original $H$.
-   **Formant shifting**: multiply by the warped envelope $H(\omega / \gamma)$ instead, which changes the perceived size of the speaker.
-   **Envelope transfer** (cross-synthesis): multiply the excitation of one sound by the envelope of another.

The envelope is estimated by cepstral liftering (Proposition 1.5) or by linear prediction (LPC), which fits an all-pole filter $G / |A(e^{i\omega})|$ by solving the Yule–Walker equations (ch. 11).
:::

```python
import numpy as np

fs, N, Ra = 16000, 1024, 256                  # Hann window, analysis hop N/4
w = np.hanning(N + 1)[:N]
omega = 2 * np.pi * np.arange(N // 2 + 1) / N  # bin centre frequencies (rad/sample)
princarg = lambda p: (p + np.pi) % (2 * np.pi) - np.pi

def phase_vocoder(x, alpha):
    """Time-scale modification by a factor alpha (> 1 = slower), pitch unchanged."""
    Rs = int(round(alpha * Ra))
    frames = [np.fft.rfft(x[i:i + N] * w) for i in range(0, len(x) - N, Ra)]
    y = np.zeros(Rs * len(frames) + N); norm = np.zeros_like(y)
    psi = np.angle(frames[0])
    for m, X in enumerate(frames):
        if m > 0:
            dphi = np.angle(X) - np.angle(frames[m - 1]) - omega * Ra
            inst = omega + princarg(dphi) / Ra       # instantaneous frequency per bin
            psi = psi + Rs * inst                    # phase propagation at the synthesis hop
        frame = np.fft.irfft(np.abs(X) * np.exp(1j * psi), n=N) * w
        y[m * Rs:m * Rs + N] += frame; norm[m * Rs:m * Rs + N] += w ** 2
    return y / np.maximum(norm, 1e-3)

def peaks(x, k=2):
    X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x * np.hanning(len(x)), 8 * len(x)))
    f = np.fft.rfftfreq(8 * len(x), 1 / fs)
    loc = [i for i in range(1, len(X) - 1) if X[i] >= X[i - 1] and X[i] > X[i + 1]]
    return np.sort(f[sorted(loc, key=lambda i: -X[i])[:k]]).round(1)

t = np.arange(fs) / fs                             # 1 s of a two-note chord
x = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 440 * t) + 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 660 * t + 1)
y = phase_vocoder(x, 1.5)
print(f"duration {len(x) / fs:.2f} s -> {len(y) / fs:.2f} s; peaks {peaks(x)} -> {peaks(y[N:-N])} Hz")

beta = 2 ** (4 / 12)                               # pitch shift by a major third
z = phase_vocoder(x, beta)
z = np.interp(np.arange(0, len(z) - 1, beta), np.arange(len(z)), z)   # resample by 1/beta
print(f"pitch shift: duration {len(z) / fs:.2f} s, peaks {peaks(z[N:-N])} Hz "
      f"(expected {np.round(440 * beta, 1)} and {np.round(660 * beta, 1)})")
```

The stretched chord lasts 1.48 s (1.5 s minus the edge frames) with its peaks still at 440 and 660 Hz. The pitch-shifted version lasts 1.00 s with peaks at 554.4 and 831.5 Hz, as predicted. Linear interpolation is a crude resampler; a polyphase filter (`scipy.signal.resample_poly`) is better for listening.

The second block estimates the envelope of a synthetic vowel (formants at 700 and 1200 Hz, pitch 120 Hz) both ways.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import lfilter, freqz
from scipy.linalg import solve_toeplitz

fs, f0 = 16000, 120
# Source-filter vowel: impulse train through two resonances (formants at 700 and 1200 Hz)
poles = []
for F, B in ((700, 80), (1200, 100)):
    r = np.exp(-np.pi * B / fs)
    poles += [r * np.exp(2j * np.pi * F / fs), r * np.exp(-2j * np.pi * F / fs)]
a_true = np.real(np.poly(poles))
e = np.zeros(fs // 2); e[::fs // f0] = 1.0
x = lfilter([1.0], a_true, e)

seg = x[2000:2000 + 1024] * np.hanning(1024)
# 1. Cepstral envelope: keep quefrencies below the pitch period (fs/f0 = 133 samples)
logS = np.log(np.abs(np.fft.fft(seg, 4096)) + 1e-9)
c = np.fft.ifft(logS).real
lifter = np.zeros(4096); lifter[:50] = 1; lifter[-49:] = 1
env_cep = np.exp(np.fft.fft(c * lifter).real[:2049])
# 2. LPC envelope of order 8 (autocorrelation method, Yule-Walker equations)
r = np.correlate(seg, seg, "full")[1023:1023 + 9]
a = solve_toeplitz(r[:8], -r[1:9])
f, Hl = freqz([1.0], np.r_[1, a], worN=2049, fs=fs)
for name, env in (("cepstrum", env_cep), ("LPC", np.abs(Hl))):
    pk = [i for i in range(1, 600) if env[i] > env[i - 1] and env[i] > env[i + 1]]
    print(f"{name:8s} envelope peaks below 2400 Hz: {np.round(f[pk])} Hz")
```

The cepstral envelope peaks at 726 and 1163 Hz and the LPC envelope at 711 and 1199 Hz. A shorter lifter (20 coefficients) smooths the two formants into a single peak, the usual trade-off between smoothness and detail.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   Resampling scales time and frequency together; pitch shifting is a time stretch followed by resampling.
-   The phase vocoder re-synthesises each bin at its instantaneous frequency; it is exact for stationary sinusoids when $R_a \le N/4$ with a Hann window.
-   Phase locking reduces phasiness; WSOLA and PSOLA are time-domain alternatives for speech.
-   Timbre lives in the spectral envelope, estimated by cepstral liftering or linear prediction; separating it from the excitation preserves formants or transfers timbre.
:::

## 6. Spatial audio: binaural, transaural and wave field synthesis {#ch6}

3D rendering makes a listener hear a sound at a chosen position. Perceptual approaches reproduce the signals at the two eardrums; physical approaches reproduce the sound field over a whole area. This chapter derives both, with their limits.

### Localisation cues

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Interaural cues]{.tag} A source at azimuth $\theta$ reaches the two ears with an **interaural time difference** (ITD) and an **interaural level difference** (ILD). For a rigid spherical head of radius $a$ and a distant source, Woodworth's formula gives
$$
\mathrm{ITD}(\theta) = \frac{a}{c}\, (\theta + \sin\theta), \qquad 0 \le \theta \le \pi / 2,
$$
with $c \approx 343$ m/s.
:::

With $a = 8.75$ cm the ITD reaches 0.66 ms at 90°. The ITD dominates below about 1.5 kHz, and the ILD, caused by head shadowing, above it (the duplex theory). Both cues are equal for all directions on a **cone of confusion**; the spectral filtering of the pinnae resolves front–back and elevation ambiguities.

### Head-related transfer functions and binaural synthesis

::: def
[Definition 6.2 — HRTF and binaural synthesis]{.tag} The head-related transfer function $H_{L}(f, \theta, \phi)$ is the ratio of the sound pressure at the left eardrum (or at the blocked ear canal) to the free-field pressure at the centre of the head, for a source at azimuth $\theta$ and elevation $\phi$; similarly $H_R$. Their inverse transforms are head-related impulse responses (HRIRs).

**Binaural synthesis** renders a mono source $s$ at $(\theta, \phi)$ over headphones by filtering it with the two HRIRs:
$$
y_L = h_L^{\theta, \phi} * s, \qquad y_R = h_R^{\theta, \phi} * s .
$$
:::

HRTFs are measured on dummy heads such as KEMAR (Gardner and Martin, 1995) or on people (the CIPIC database, Algazi et al., 2001), on a grid of directions; rendering a moving source interpolates between them. Non-individual HRTFs cause front–back confusions and sounds perceived inside the head. Head tracking, which keeps the virtual source fixed in the room, reduces both.

### Transaural reproduction

Transaural rendering plays binaural signals over two loudspeakers. Each ear hears both loudspeakers, so the crosstalk must be cancelled.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.3 — Crosstalk cancellation]{.tag} At frequency $f$, let $\mathbf{G}(f)$ be the $2 \times 2$ matrix of transfer functions from the loudspeakers to the ears, and $\mathbf{b}$ the desired binaural signals. The loudspeaker feeds $\mathbf{C}\mathbf{b}$ give the ear signals $\mathbf{G}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{b}$.

They equal $\mathbf{b}$ when $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{G}^{-1}$. The regularised filter of Kirkeby, Nelson and Hamada (1998) limits the loudspeaker gains where $\mathbf{G}$ is ill-conditioned:
$$
\mathbf{C}_\beta = (\mathbf{G}^H \mathbf{G} + \beta \mathbf{I})^{-1} \mathbf{G}^H .
$$
In the symmetric case, with ipsilateral and contralateral paths $G_i$ and $G_c$,
$$
\mathbf{G}^{-1} = \frac{1}{G_i^2 - G_c^2} \begin{pmatrix} G_i & -G_c \\ -G_c & G_i \end{pmatrix},
$$
which is singular whenever $G_c = \pm G_i$.

::: proof
The regularised filter is the Tikhonov solution: for every $\mathbf{b}$, the feed $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{C}_\beta \mathbf{b}$ minimises
$$
\|\mathbf{G}\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{b}\|^2 + \beta\, \|\mathbf{u}\|^2 .
$$
The inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix is its adjugate divided by its determinant, here $G_i^2 - G_c^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In free field, $G_c \approx G_i\, e^{-2i\pi f \Delta / c}$, where $\Delta$ is the path difference between the far and the near loudspeaker. The inverse then blows up at low frequency and at the multiples of $c / 2\Delta$. The cancellation also holds only in a small "sweet spot" around the assumed head position.

### Wave field synthesis

Wave field synthesis (Berkhout, de Vries and Vogel, 1993) reproduces a sound field inside a region by Huygens' principle: a wavefront can be re-emitted by secondary sources placed on a surface.

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.4 — Kirchhoff–Helmholtz integral]{.tag} Let $P$ satisfy the Helmholtz equation $\Delta P + k^2 P = 0$ in a bounded region $V$ with smooth boundary $\partial V$ and outward normal $\mathbf{n}$.

Let $G$ be the free-field Green's function, with $r = \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0\|$:
$$
G(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{x}_0) = \frac{e^{-ik r}}{4\pi r} .
$$
Then for $\mathbf{x} \in V$,
$$
P(\mathbf{x}) = \oint_{\partial V} \Big[ G(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{x}_0)\, \frac{\partial P}{\partial n}(\mathbf{x}_0) - P(\mathbf{x}_0)\, \frac{\partial G}{\partial n}(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{x}_0) \Big]\, dS(\mathbf{x}_0) .
$$
The field inside $V$ is thus produced by monopoles (first term) and dipoles (second term) on $\partial V$, driven by the boundary values of the field.

::: proof
$G$ satisfies $\Delta G + k^2 G = -\delta_{\mathbf{x}}$. Green's second identity on $V$ gives
$$
\int_V (G\, \Delta P - P\, \Delta G)\, dV = \oint_{\partial V} \Big( G\, \frac{\partial P}{\partial n} - P\, \frac{\partial G}{\partial n} \Big)\, dS .
$$
On the left, $\Delta P = -k^2 P$ and $\Delta G = -k^2 G - \delta_{\mathbf{x}}$, so the integrand reduces to $P\, \delta_{\mathbf{x}}$ and the integral to $P(\mathbf{x})$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For a plane boundary, choosing a Green's function with zero normal derivative on the plane removes the dipoles and doubles the monopoles: this is the **Rayleigh I integral**. A virtual source behind the plane is rendered in the half-space in front by monopoles with driving function $-2\, \partial P / \partial n$, the normal now pointing into the listening region. WFS samples this layer with a line of loudspeakers.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.5 — Spatial aliasing]{.tag} Loudspeakers spaced $\Delta x$ apart on a line, rendering a plane wave whose direction makes the angle $\theta$ with the normal of the array, reproduce it without spatial aliasing only below
$$
f_{\mathrm{al}}(\theta) = \frac{c}{\Delta x\, (1 + |\sin\theta|)} .
$$
Over all directions the safe bound is $c / 2\Delta x$.

::: proof
The driving signals vary along the array as $e^{-i k x \sin\theta}$. Sampling them every $\Delta x$ replicates their spatial spectrum at the wavenumbers $k\sin\theta + 2\pi m / \Delta x$.

A replica with $|k_x| < k$ is a propagating plane wave in another direction (a grating lobe). The nearest replica, $m = \pm 1$, propagates when $2\pi / \Delta x - k|\sin\theta| < k$, that is when $f > f_{\mathrm{al}}(\theta)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With 15 cm between loudspeakers, waves arriving at 45° alias above 1339 Hz. Above $f_{\mathrm{al}}$ the field is wrong, although listeners still localise reasonably well thanks to the precedence effect.

```python
import numpy as np

c, a = 343.0, 0.0875                                  # speed of sound (m/s), head radius (m)
# 1. Woodworth's interaural time difference
for deg in (0, 30, 60, 90):
    th = np.radians(deg)
    print(f"azimuth {deg:2d} deg: ITD = {1e3 * a / c * (th + np.sin(th)):.3f} ms")

# 2. Crosstalk cancellation, free-field model: loudspeakers at +-30 deg, 2 m; ears at +-a
ears = np.array([[-a, 0.0], [a, 0.0]])
spk = 2.0 * np.array([[-np.sin(np.pi / 6), np.cos(np.pi / 6)], [np.sin(np.pi / 6), np.cos(np.pi / 6)]])
dist = np.linalg.norm(ears[:, None, :] - spk[None, :, :], axis=2)    # ear x loudspeaker
def G(f):                                            # acoustic transfer matrix (point sources)
    k = 2 * np.pi * f / c
    return np.exp(-1j * k * dist) / (4 * np.pi * dist)
delta = dist[0, 1] - dist[0, 0]                       # contralateral minus ipsilateral path
print(f"path difference {100 * delta:.2f} cm: G is singular at multiples of c/(2 delta) = {c / (2 * delta):.0f} Hz")
for f in (100, 1000, 1900, 3000):
    Gf = G(f)
    beta = 1e-3 * np.linalg.norm(Gf, 2) ** 2           # Tikhonov regularisation
    Cf = np.linalg.solve(Gf.conj().T @ Gf + beta * np.eye(2), Gf.conj().T)
    E = Gf @ Cf                                       # ear signals = E @ binaural signals
    sep = 20 * np.log10(np.abs(E[0, 0]) / np.abs(E[1, 0]))
    effort = 20 * np.log10(np.linalg.norm(Cf, 2) * np.linalg.norm(Gf, 2))
    print(f"f = {f:4d} Hz: cond(G) = {np.linalg.cond(Gf):6.1f}, separation {sep:5.1f} dB, "
          f"filter gain {effort:5.1f} dB")

# 3. Wave field synthesis of a plane wave with a line of monopoles (Rayleigh I, 2.5D)
dx = 0.15                                             # loudspeaker spacing (m)
xs = np.arange(-4, 4 + 1e-9, dx)
grid = np.array([(u, v) for u in np.linspace(-0.5, 0.5, 11) for v in np.linspace(1, 2, 11)])
r = np.linalg.norm(grid[:, None, :] - np.c_[xs, 0 * xs][None], axis=2)
for deg in (0, 45):
    th = np.radians(deg)
    print(f"plane wave at {deg} deg: aliasing above c / (dx (1 + sin)) = {c / (dx * (1 + np.sin(th))):.0f} Hz")
    for f in (500, 1000, 2000, 4000):
        k = 2 * np.pi * f / c
        drive = np.exp(-1j * k * xs * np.sin(th))           # delays of the incoming wave
        p = (drive * np.exp(-1j * k * r) / (4 * np.pi * r)).sum(1)
        target = np.exp(-1j * k * (grid[:, 0] * np.sin(th) + grid[:, 1] * np.cos(th)))
        gain = np.vdot(target, p) / np.vdot(target, target)   # best complex scale
        err = np.linalg.norm(p - gain * target) / np.linalg.norm(gain * target)
        print(f"   f = {f:4d} Hz: relative error of the synthesised field {err:.2f}")
```

The ITDs are 0.26, 0.49 and 0.66 ms at 30°, 60° and 90°. The crosstalk canceller is well conditioned at 1000 and 3000 Hz (channel separation 90 and 80 dB, no extra gain), but at 100 Hz and near 1961 Hz its conditioning collapses: separation falls to 24 and 17 dB despite 20–23 dB of extra filter gain.

The line array reproduces the frontal plane wave with a relative error of 0.12–0.18 up to 2000 Hz and 1.60 at 4000 Hz, beyond its aliasing frequency of 2287 Hz. For the wave at 45°, the error is 0.16 at 1000 Hz and 0.89 at 2000 Hz, beyond 1339 Hz. The residual 12 % below aliasing comes from the finite array and from using a line (the "2.5D" amplitude error).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 6

-   Interaural time and level differences locate sources in azimuth; pinna filtering, captured by HRTFs, adds elevation and front–back cues.
-   Binaural synthesis convolves a source with a pair of HRIRs; transaural rendering adds a crosstalk canceller, ill-conditioned at low frequency and at multiples of $c / 2\Delta$.
-   The Kirchhoff–Helmholtz integral reproduces a field inside a region from monopoles and dipoles on its boundary; WFS keeps the monopoles (Rayleigh I).
-   A loudspeaker spacing $\Delta x$ limits WFS to frequencies below $c / (\Delta x (1 + |\sin\theta|))$.
:::

## 7. Source separation I: linear and convolutive mixtures {#ch7}

Source separation, or demixing, recovers the signals of several sources from recordings of their mixture. This chapter treats the case with at least as many microphones as sources, where the mixture can be inverted once it is identified, blindly, from the statistics of the sources.

### Mixing models

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Mixing models]{.tag} Let $J$ sources $s_j$ be recorded by $M$ microphones $x_i$.

-   **Instantaneous** (linear) mixture: $\mathbf{x}(n) = \mathbf{A}\, \mathbf{s}(n)$, with an $M \times J$ mixing matrix $\mathbf{A}$; studio panning produces such mixtures.
-   **Anechoic** mixture: $x_i(n) = \sum_j a_{ij}\, s_j(n - \delta_{ij})$, with gains and delays only.
-   **Convolutive** mixture: $x_i(n) = \sum_j (a_{ij} * s_j)(n)$, with room impulse responses $a_{ij}$.

The mixture is **determined** when $M = J$, overdetermined when $M > J$ and **underdetermined** when $M < J$ (ch. 8). The contribution of source $j$ to all microphones is its **spatial image**.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 7.2 — Ambiguities]{.tag} For any permutation matrix $\mathbf{P}$ and invertible diagonal matrix $\mathbf{D}$, the mixing matrix and sources
$$
\mathbf{A}' = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{P}^{-1}, \qquad \mathbf{s}' = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{s}
$$
produce the same mixture as $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{s})$. Blind separation can therefore recover the sources only up to order and scale.
:::

### Independent component analysis

The blind assumption is that the sources are mutually independent. Second-order statistics alone do not suffice.

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.3 — Whitening leaves a rotation]{.tag} Let $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}$ with $\mathbf{A}$ square invertible and uncorrelated sources of unit variance. Let $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{x}$ be white, $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}\mathbf{z}^\top] = \mathbf{I}$. Then $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{s}$ with $\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}$ orthogonal.

If the sources are Gaussian, $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{s}$ has the same distribution for every orthogonal $\mathbf{Q}$, so no method can identify the rotation.

::: proof
Since the sources are uncorrelated with unit variance,
$$
\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}\mathbf{z}^\top] = \mathbf{Q}\, \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{s}\mathbf{s}^\top]\, \mathbf{Q}^\top = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^\top = \mathbf{I} .
$$
A standard Gaussian vector is invariant under orthogonal maps. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 7.4 — Identifiability (Comon, 1994)]{.tag} Let $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}$ with $\mathbf{A}$ invertible and independent sources, at most one of them Gaussian. If $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$ has independent components, then
$$
\mathbf{W}\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}
$$
for a permutation $\mathbf{P}$ and an invertible diagonal $\mathbf{D}$. The proof rests on the Darmois–Skitovich theorem; see Comon (1994).
:::

::: def
[Definition 7.5 — Contrasts and FastICA]{.tag} ICA maximises a measure of non-Gaussianity of the outputs, called a contrast: negentropy, or for a unit-variance output the **kurtosis** $\kappa(y) = \mathbb{E}[y^4] - 3$. Speech and music are super-Gaussian ($\kappa > 0$).

On whitened data, **FastICA** (Hyvärinen and Oja, 2000) iterates, for one unit vector $\mathbf{w}$,
$$
\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{z}\, (\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{z})^3\big] - 3\mathbf{w}, \qquad \mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} / \|\mathbf{w}\|,
$$
and extracts further components orthogonally to the previous ones.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.6 — FastICA converges cubically]{.tag} Write $\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{Q}^\top \mathbf{w}$, the coordinates of $\mathbf{w}$ in the source basis. One iteration of Definition 7.5 maps each coordinate to $q_i \mapsto \kappa(s_i)\, q_i^3$, before normalisation. From almost every starting point, $\mathbf{q}$ converges to a signed unit vector $\pm \mathbf{e}_i$, that is, $\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{z} = \pm s_i$, and the convergence is cubic.

::: proof
Since $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{s}$, the output is $\mathbf{q}^\top \mathbf{s}$ and the update in source coordinates is
$$
\mathbf{q} \leftarrow \mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{s}\, (\mathbf{q}^\top \mathbf{s})^3\big] - 3\mathbf{q} .
$$
Expanding the cube, independence, zero means and unit variances give
$$
\mathbb{E}\Big[s_i \Big(\sum_j q_j s_j\Big)^3\Big] = q_i^3\, \mathbb{E}[s_i^4] + 3 q_i \sum_{j \ne i} q_j^2 = q_i^3\, (\mathbb{E}[s_i^4] - 3) + 3 q_i\, \|\mathbf{q}\|^2 .
$$
With $\|\mathbf{q}\| = 1$, subtracting $3 q_i$ leaves $\kappa(s_i)\, q_i^3$.

Cubing amplifies the largest $|\kappa(s_i)|^{1/2} |q_i|$ relative to the others; after normalisation the ratios $q_j / q_i$ are cubed at each step. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Maximum-likelihood ICA, which updates the whole demixing matrix at once, is presented in ch. 11.

### Convolutive mixtures in the frequency domain

::: prop
[Proposition 7.7 — Narrowband approximation]{.tag} If the mixing filters are short compared with the STFT window, the convolutive mixture becomes an instantaneous mixture in each frequency bin:
$$
\mathbf{x}(m, k) \approx \mathbf{A}(k)\, \mathbf{s}(m, k),
$$
where $\mathbf{A}(k)$ holds the frequency responses of the filters. The relation is exact for circular convolution (Proposition 0.2); for linear convolution the error comes from the samples near the frame edges, a fraction of the frame of the order of the filter length divided by $N$.
:::

**Frequency-domain ICA** separates each bin with complex-valued ICA (Smaragdis, 1998). Proposition 7.2 now applies *per bin*. Each bin returns the sources in its own order (the **permutation problem**), which is resolved by aligning the bins on the correlation of the source envelopes across frequencies or on the directions of arrival.

Each bin also has its own scale, which the minimal distortion principle fixes:
$$
\mathbf{W}(k) \leftarrow \mathrm{diag}\big(\mathbf{W}(k)^{-1}\big)\, \mathbf{W}(k) .
$$
Each output is then the spatial image of its source on one microphone.

### Measuring separation quality

::: def
[Definition 7.8 — SDR, SIR and SAR]{.tag} Following Vincent, Gribonval and Févotte (2006), decompose an estimate as
$$
\hat s_j = s_{\mathrm{target}} + e_{\mathrm{interf}} + e_{\mathrm{artif}},
$$
where $s_{\mathrm{target}}$ is its projection on the true source $s_j$ and $e_{\mathrm{interf}}$ the projection of the rest on the other sources. Then
$$
\mathrm{SDR} = 10 \log_{10} \frac{\|s_{\mathrm{target}}\|^2}{\|e_{\mathrm{interf}} + e_{\mathrm{artif}}\|^2}, \qquad \mathrm{SIR} = 10 \log_{10} \frac{\|s_{\mathrm{target}}\|^2}{\|e_{\mathrm{interf}}\|^2},
$$
and the SAR compares $s_{\mathrm{target}} + e_{\mathrm{interf}}$ with $e_{\mathrm{artif}}$ in the same way, all in decibels.
:::

The code mixes a sawtooth and a modulated Laplacian noise with a fixed $2 \times 2$ matrix, compares whitening alone with FastICA, then measures the narrowband error for a 32 ms room-like filter.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import FastICA, PCA
from scipy.signal import lfilter

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
fs = 8000
t = np.arange(2 * fs) / fs
s1 = 2 * ((110 * t) % 1) - 1                                   # sawtooth (sub-Gaussian)
s2 = rng.laplace(size=len(t)) * (0.6 + 0.4 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 3 * t))   # speech-like, super-Gaussian
S = np.c_[s1, s2] / np.c_[s1, s2].std(0)
A = np.array([[1.0, 0.6], [0.5, 1.0]])
X = S @ A.T                                                     # instantaneous mixture x = A s

def sir_db(Y, S):
    """Signal-to-interference ratio after resolving permutation and scale."""
    C = np.abs(np.corrcoef(Y.T, S.T)[:2, 2:])                    # |corr(y_i, s_j)|
    perm = [0, 1] if C[0, 0] + C[1, 1] > C[0, 1] + C[1, 0] else [1, 0]
    out = []
    for i, j in enumerate(perm):
        G = np.linalg.lstsq(S, Y[:, i], rcond=None)[0]         # y_i = G_j s_j + G_other s_other
        out.append(20 * np.log10(abs(G[j]) / abs(G[1 - j])))
    return np.round(out, 1)

print("mixtures      SIR (dB):", sir_db(X, S))
print("PCA whitening SIR (dB):", sir_db(PCA(2, whiten=True).fit_transform(X), S))
print("FastICA       SIR (dB):", sir_db(FastICA(2, whiten="unit-variance", random_state=0).fit_transform(X), S))

# Narrowband approximation of a convolutive mixture: X(m,k) ~ A(k) S(m,k)?
h = rng.standard_normal(256) * np.exp(-np.arange(256) / 40)   # a 32 ms room-like filter
s = rng.standard_normal(4 * fs)
xconv = lfilter(h, [1.0], s)
for N in (256, 1024, 4096):
    w = np.hanning(N)
    fr = lambda z: np.array([np.fft.rfft(z[i:i + N] * w) for i in range(N, len(z) - N, N // 4)])
    Xs, Ss = fr(xconv), fr(s)
    Hk = np.fft.rfft(h, N)
    err = np.linalg.norm(Xs - Hk * Ss) / np.linalg.norm(Xs)
    print(f"window {N:4d} samples: relative error of X = H S per bin: {err:.2f}")
```

The mixtures have SIRs of 4.4 and 6.0 dB. Whitening alone gives 0.4 dB: it decorrelates, but the remaining rotation mixes the sources again (Proposition 7.3). FastICA reaches 42.5 and 44.1 dB. The narrowband relative error falls from 0.36 to 0.10 and 0.02 as the window grows from 256 to 1024 and 4096 samples.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 7

-   Mixtures are instantaneous, anechoic or convolutive, and determined, over- or underdetermined; sources are recovered only up to permutation and scale.
-   Whitening leaves an unknown rotation; independence and non-Gaussianity identify it (Comon's theorem).
-   FastICA maximises kurtosis by a cubically convergent fixed point.
-   Convolutive mixtures become per-bin instantaneous mixtures, at the price of per-bin permutation and scale ambiguities; SDR, SIR and SAR measure the result.
:::

## 8. Source separation II: underdetermined and sparse models, DUET {#ch8}

With fewer microphones than sources, the mixing matrix has no inverse and independence is not enough. The extra assumption that makes separation possible is sparsity: in the time–frequency plane, few sources are active at each point.

### Sparsity in the time–frequency plane

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — W-disjoint orthogonality]{.tag} Sources are W-disjoint orthogonal (Jourjine, Rickard and Yilmaz, 2000) when, for the STFT with window $W$, at most one of them is non-zero at each time–frequency point:
$$
S_j(m, k)\, S_l(m, k) = 0 \quad \text{for all } j \ne l \text{ and all } (m, k) .
$$
Speech approximately satisfies this: harmonics of different voices rarely overlap, and voices pause.
:::

Then each time–frequency point belongs to one source, and separation reduces to classifying points and masking. A softer version of the assumption is a sparse prior: each coefficient follows a heavy-tailed density, such as the Laplacian, whose maximum a posteriori estimate penalises the ℓ1 norm.

:::: prop
